fetched_contents.text: Simultaneous quantitation of structurally analogous bile acid isomers via charge-state-engineered UPLC-MS Author affiliations * Corresponding authors a Fujian Key Laboratory of Agro-Products Quality and Safety, Institute of Quality Standards and Testing Technology for Agro-products, Fujian Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Fuzhou, China E-mail: sudesen@hotmail.com Tel: +86 0591 87861853 b Ministry of Education Key Laboratory for Analytical Science of Food Safety and Biology, and College of Chemistry, Fuzhou University, Fuzhou, Fujian 350108, China Abstract Ursodeoxycholic, hyodeoxycholic, chenodeoxycholic, and deoxycholic acids are endogenous, dihydroxylated bile acid isomers that share a molecular mass but fulfill specific biological roles. However, their isomeric structures complicate analytical separation, while low physiological concentrations demand high detection sensitivity. Consequently, despite the use of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry for simultaneous analysis, current methodologies are often hampered by inadequate sensitivity and lengthy analysis durations. To address this analytical bottleneck, we developed an ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS) method for the quantitative analysis of four bile acid isomers. This method employs a novel charge-state homogenization strategy, guided by computational prediction of ionization behavior (pH/ionic forms), to optimize chromatographic and mass spectrometric conditions. By inducing complete deprotonation and generating uniform carboxylate anions for all analytes, this approach synergistically enhances the detection sensitivity, chromatographic resolution, and analysis speed. The rigorously validated method demonstrates exceptional performance: sub-ng mL−1 sensitivity (LODs 0.10–0.22 ng mL−1), rapid analysis (<8 min), excellent linearity (R2 > 0.998 over 4 orders of magnitude), high reproducibility (intra/inter-day RSD 1.2–9.1%), and satisfactory accuracy (86.1–107.1% recovery). Its broad applicability was confirmed across diverse matrices (poultry/porcine blood, bile, concentrates), handling trace to high bile acid levels. This rapid, sensitive and highly-resolutive analytical approach addresses key challenges in bile acid isomers quantitation, offering significant advantages for pharmacokinetic research and quality control in animal health and pharmaceutical applications. Furthermore, the underlying charge-state homogenization principle provides a rational framework for optimizing chromatographic parameters (organic modifiers, stationary phases, gradients) in complex analyses. Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2019 Jun 6. Published in final edited form as: Anal Bioanal Chem. 2017 Jul 8;409(23):5533–5545. doi: 10.1007/s00216-017-0489-1 Abstract Bile acids (BAs) are cholesterol metabolites with important biological functions. They undergo extensive host-gut microbial co-metabolisms during the enterohepatic circulation, creating a vast structural diversity and resulting in great challenges to separate and detect them. Based on the bioanalytical reports in the past decade, this work developed three chromatographic gradient methods to separate a total of 48 BA standards on BEH C18 column and HSS T3 column and accordingly unraveled the factors affecting the separation and detection of them by liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (LC-MS). It was presented that both the acidity and ammonium levels in mobile phases reduced the electrospray ionization (ESI) of BAs as anions of [M-H]-, especially for those unconjugated ones without 12-hydroxylation. It was also found that the retention of taurine-conjugates on BEH C18 column was sensitive to the strength of formic acid and ammonium in mobile phases. By using the volatile buffers with an equivalent ammonium level as mobile phases, we comprehensively demonstrated the effects of the elution pH value on the retention behaviors of BAs on both BEH C18 column and HSS T3 column. Based on the retention data acquired on C18 column, we presented the ionization constants (pKa) of various BAs with the widest coverage beyond previous reports. When we made attempts to establish the structure-retention relationships (SRR) of BAs, the lack of discriminative structural descriptors for BA stereoisomers emerged as the bottleneck problem. The methods and results presented in this work are especially useful for the development a reliable, sensitive, high-throughput and robust LC-MS bioanalytical protocols for the quantitative metabolomic studies. Keywords: High Performance Liquid Chromatography, Mass Spectrometry, Bile acid, Electrospray ionization, Ionization constant, Structure-retention relationship 1. Introduction Human Bile acids (BAs) are C24 molecules comprised of a C19 cyclopentanophenanthrene (steroid) nucleus and a carboxylate side-chain. They are cholesterol metabolites undergoing extensive enterohepatic circulation driven by a series of host-gut microbial metabolism and transport mechanisms [1–3]. During exchanges between the host and gut microbiota, BAs act on both of them and plays multiple biological roles [4–10]. The metabolomic profile of BAs therefore manifests a footprint of host-gut microbial interactions that are closely associated with health and diseases. However, the highly interactive disposition of BAs by the host and gut microbiota produces a vast structural diversity (Fig. 1 and Table S1) associated with (1) A/B ring fusion stereochemistry (trans/5α-H or cis/5β-H); (2) sites of hydroxylation at C3, C6, C7 and/or C12; (3) dehydrogenation and epimerization of the hydroxyl groups; and (4) conjugation of glycine or taurine at the C24-carboxyl group and/or conjugation of glucuronide or sulfate at hydroxyl/ C24-carboxyl groups [11]. It is challenging to separate and detect such a great deal of BAs in biological samples with such a small structural difference but disparate physicochemical properties. Liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (LC-MS) is currently prevailing in BAs analysis [12]. In a typical LC-MS method, BAs are separated by reverse chromatography, ionized by the negative electrospray ionization (ESI-), and detected by multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). Owing to the occurrence of a lot of isomers and stereoisomers, it’s difficult to differentiate them with current tandem mass spectrometric techniques. A pseudo-MRM method has to be employed for the unconjugated isomers, such as CDCA/HDCA, and most of unconjugated stereoisomers, such as LCA/isoLCA, CDCA/UDCA/βUDCA, HDCA/βHDCA/muroCA and HCA/αMCA/βMCA/ωMCA. All these unconjugated BAs have no 12-hydroxyl group. They fragmented merely via dehydration and dehydrogenation and exhibit none discriminative fragments regardless of sites and epimerization of the hydroxyl groups on the skeleton [13]. We have characterized a distinctive framentation mechanism for the 12-hydroxylated unconjugated ones, such as DCA and CA. The 12-hydroxyl group induces the rotation of the carboxylate side chain and the proton transfer between 12-hydroxyl group and 24-carboxyl group. The subsequent dissociation routes enable the discrimination of 12-hydroxylated ones from the others with MRM method [13]. For the conjugated BAs, such as glycine-conjugates and taurine-conjugates, the dissociations of the steroid nucleus have been obscured by the signals derived from cleavage of the amide side chain [13]. As a result, isomers and stereoisomers of conjugated BAs may also not be discriminated by MRM method. In summary, the discrimination of the unknown BAs from the known ones relies heavily on the separation power and the robustness of chromatography. It is crucial to disclose the fundamental factors affecting the separation and detection of them and accordingly establish structure-retention relationships (SRR). fetched_contents.text: Modified aqueous mobile phases: A way to improve retention behavior of active pharmaceutical compounds and their impurities in liquid chromatography Under a Creative Commons license Open access Highlights * • Mobile phase modification in RP-HPLC as a solution for common analytical challenges. * • * • Abstract Most commonly used analytical technique for determination of active pharmaceutical ingredients and their impurities in quality control throughout all phases of drug research, development and manufacture is definitely reversed-phase high performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC). However, pharmaceutical industry professionals are often faced with various challenges in RP mode, which cannot be resolved with common variations in the composition of the mobile phase. These challenges often occur when analyzing compounds that contain basic ionizable groups, possess large differences in polarities and require consumption of high amounts of toxic organic solvents. Among available strategies for addressing the aforementioned issues, the most convenient one includes RP-HPLC mobile phase modifications by an addition of the proper chemical compounds. In that respect, RP-HPLC method can be easily adapted to the needs of the analysis without time-consuming and expensive equipment procurement. In this review the chaotropic chromatography, micellar liquid chromatography, and cyclodextrin modified RP-HPLC systems are presented and discussed in details. The mobile-phase pH strongly influences chromatographic separation of bile acids by altering retention, selectivity, peak shape, and resolution. The evidence points to a central mechanism: protonation/deprotonation changes the ionization state of bile acids, which in turn modifies their interaction with the stationary phase and overall retention behavior.

First, protonation and deprotonation directly change retention and selectivity. A general chromatography source states that “the mobile-phase pH can be a powerful tool to control retention and selectivity” [N1-R1], and a more specific bile acid study emphasizes that mobile-phase pH affects retention behaviors and negative electrospray ionization of bile acids [N3-F2]. The same source also notes that “the acidity and ammonium levels in mobile phases reduced the electrospray ionization (ESI) of BAs as anions of [M-H]−, especially for those unconjugated ones without 12-hydroxylation” [N3-F2]. This indicates that the pH is not only a retention control parameter but also a key determinant of analyte ionization state, which is central to selectivity differences across bile acid isomers and conjugates [N1-R1]. Another source explains that “the ionization state determines... the retention and selectivity” [N4-R5], reinforcing the idea that protonation/deprotonation is the underlying mechanism by which pH controls chromatographic behavior.

Second, mobile-phase pH affects interaction with the stationary phase. Mobile-phase modifications can “modify the analytes retention and selectivity” [N1-R3], and the chromatography review explicitly says that mobile-phase pH can “affect chromatography in a number of ways” and should be chosen “to optimize retention and selectivity during method” [N1-R4]. In bile acid analysis, the study reports that “the retention of taurine-conjugates on BEH C18 column was sensitive to the strength of formic acid and ammonium in mobile phases” [N3-F2]. This suggests that pH changes alter the effective strength of the mobile-phase buffer and modifier, thereby changing the hydrophobicity or charge distribution of the analyte and how it interacts with the stationary phase [N4-F3]. The chromatography review further explains that mobile-phase composition, including pH, “provides the RP-HPLC methods with the ability to modulate the analytes’ retention and separation” [N4-F3]. That is especially important for bile acids, which have a wide structural diversity and can show substantial differences in retention depending on their functional groups and ionization state [N3-F2].

Third, pH impacts peak shape and resolution in bile acid separations. The chromatography source notes that lowering mobile-phase pH can improve either peak shape or separation selectivity [N1-R5]. The bile acid study explicitly states that “by using the volatile buffers with an equivalent ammonium level as mobile phases, we comprehensively demonstrated the effects of the elution pH value on the retention behaviors of BAs” [N3-F2], which implies that pH changes can lead to systematic shifts in peak retention and therefore resolution. In addition, the chromatography review emphasizes that buffers control pH to stabilize analyte ionization, improve peak shape, influence selectivity, and protect the stationary phase [N4-R3]. This directly supports the conclusion that pH is a practical parameter for improving peak quality and resolving complex bile acid mixtures [N4-R3]. The same source also says that mobile-phase composition can “modulate the analytes’ retention and separation” [N4-F3], which is relevant to the resolution of bile acids when structural differences are small but physicochemical properties differ.

Overall, the evidence supports a unified picture: mobile-phase pH changes the ionization state of bile acids, which alters retention and selectivity; it also affects the interaction between analytes and the stationary phase; and it can improve peak shape and resolution by stabilizing ionization and reducing peak broadening [N1-R1][N3-F2][N4-R3][N4-F3].

Mobile-phase pH is a major determinant of ionization efficiency and detection of bile acids. The evidence shows that pH controls the ionization state and analyte charge, which in turn controls how well bile acids are ionized and detected.

First, pH controls ionization state and analyte charge. The chromatography review states that “the pH of the mobile phase directly affects the ionization state of analytes, particularly those that are weak acids or bases” [N6-R4]. The bile acid study reports that “the acidity and ammonium levels in mobile phases reduced the electrospray ionization (ESI) of BAs as anions of [M-H]−, especially for those unconjugated ones without 12-hydroxylation” [N3-F2]. This indicates that lower acidity and higher ammonium can suppress ESI, while pH changes can shift the analyte between protonated and deprotonated forms [N3-F2]. The charge-state-engineered UPLC-MS study explicitly states that at pH ≥ 7.5, bile acids undergo complete deprotonation to form homogeneous carboxylate anions [N5-R1], which is a direct example of how pH controls analyte charge and ionization state.

Second, ionization efficiency changes with mobile-phase pH. The same UPLC-MS study reports that inducing complete deprotonation generates uniform carboxylate anions and “synergistically enhances the detection sensitivity” [N5-R1]. This suggests that ionization efficiency is not flat across pH; instead, it is maximized when the analyte is in the correct ionized form. The bile acid study also finds that ammonium levels and pH value affect the negative electrospray ionization of various bile acids [N3-F2]. That means ionization efficiency is a function of both pH and buffer chemistry, not just the analyte’s intrinsic pKa.

Third, detection response relates to ionization and mobile-phase chemistry. The UPLC-MS study states that the method employs a “charge-state homogenization strategy, guided by computational prediction of ionization behavior (pH/ionic forms), to optimize chromatographic and mass spectrometric conditions” [N5-R1]. This means that detection response is tied to the ionization state of the analyte, which is determined by pH and the mobile-phase environment. The same study notes that the method improves sensitivity, chromatographic resolution, and analysis speed by making the ionization state uniform across analytes [N5-R1]. The bile acid study similarly links mobile-phase pH and ammonium level to negative electrospray ionization and retention behavior [N3-F2], showing that detection response is not independent of the mobile-phase chemistry used.

Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that pH is a central control parameter for bile acid detection: it determines ionization state and charge, it modulates ionization efficiency, and it interacts with mobile-phase additives to shape detection response [N6-R4][N3-F2][N5-R1].

## Integrated explanation of how mobile phase pH influences chromatographic separation and ionization efficiency of bile acids

The mobile-phase pH has a fundamental and dual influence on bile acid analysis: it controls **chromatographic separation** by altering retention, selectivity, peak shape, and resolution, and it controls **ionization efficiency** by determining the ionization state and analyte charge, which in turn affects detection response. Across the branch reports, the evidence points to a unified mechanism in which pH is not merely a passive condition but an active control parameter that shapes both retention behavior and ionization/detection performance [N1-R1][N3-F2][N4-R3][N4-F3][N5-R1].

---

## 1) pH controls retention and selectivity by changing ionization state and analyte charge

The most direct way pH affects chromatographic separation is through **protonation/deprotonation**. The branch report on chromatographic separation states that mobile-phase pH can be a powerful tool to control retention and selectivity, and that the ionization state determines retention and selectivity [N1-R1][N4-R5]. A bile acid study reports that mobile-phase pH affects retention behaviors and negative electrospray ionization of bile acids [N3-F2], and that ammonium levels and pH value affect retention behaviors [N3-F2]. This means that pH changes the effective charge state of bile acids, which alters their interaction with the stationary phase and thus their retention.

The same report also notes that the retention of taurine-conjugates on BEH C18 column was sensitive to the strength of formic acid and ammonium in mobile phases [N3-F2]. This is a concrete example of how pH and buffer chemistry together modify the effective hydrophobicity and ionization state of the analyte, thereby changing retention and selectivity [N4-F3]. The chromatography review further says that mobile-phase composition, including pH, provides RP-HPLC methods with the ability to modulate retention and separation [N4-F3], reinforcing the idea that pH is a central design variable for separating bile acids.

---

## 2) pH affects interaction with the stationary phase

Mobile-phase pH affects chromatographic separation by altering the stationary-phase environment. The chromatography source notes that pH can affect chromatography in a number of ways and should be chosen to optimize retention and selectivity during method development [N1-R4]. The same source explains that mobile-phase modifications can modify retention and selectivity [N1-R3], and that buffers control pH to stabilize analyte ionization, improve peak shape, influence selectivity, ensure compatibility with detectors, and protect the stationary phase [N4-R3].

For bile acids, this means that pH is not only a retention control parameter but also a way to shape the stationary-phase chemistry. The branch report on mobile-phase additives and buffers explains that modifiers and pH interact with stationary-phase chemistry and that buffer choice affects peak quality and selectivity [N4-F3]. This is especially important because bile acids are structurally diverse and can show very different retention behavior depending on their functional groups and ionization state [N3-F2].

---

## 3) pH impacts peak shape and resolution in bile acid separations

The evidence also shows that pH can improve **peak shape** and **resolution**. A chromatography source states that lowering mobile-phase pH can improve either peak shape or separation selectivity [N1-R5]. The bile acid study reports that volatile buffers with equivalent ammonium levels were used to demonstrate the effects of elution pH on retention behaviors [N3-F2], indicating that pH changes can lead to systematic shifts in retention and thus resolution. The chromatography review further says that buffers improve peak shape and influence selectivity [N4-R3], and that mobile-phase composition can modulate retention and separation [N4-F3].

In practice, this means that pH can be tuned to reduce peak broadening and improve the separation of closely related bile acid isomers and conjugates. The branch report on chromatographic separation concludes that pH impacts peak shape and resolution in bile acid separations [N7]. That is especially valuable in bile acid analysis, where structural differences are often small but physicochemical differences can be large [N3-F2].

---

## 4) pH controls ionization state and analyte charge

On the detection side, pH is a major determinant of the analyte’s **ionization state and charge**. The branch report on ionization efficiency and detection states that the pH of the mobile phase directly affects the ionization state of analytes, particularly those that are weak acids or bases [N6-R4]. A bile acid study reports that acidity and ammonium levels in mobile phases reduced the electrospray ionization (ESI) of bile acids as anions of [M-H]−, especially for unconjugated bile acids without a 12-hydroxyl group [N3-F2]. This shows that lower acidity and higher ammonium can suppress ESI, while pH changes can shift the analyte between protonated and deprotonated forms [N3-F2].

The charge-state-engineered UPLC-MS study provides a direct example of how pH controls charge state: at pH ≥ 7.5, bile acids undergo complete deprotonation to form homogeneous carboxylate anions [N5-R1]. This uniform ionization state is important because it maximizes the likelihood of consistent ionization and improves detection response.

---

## 5) Ionization efficiency changes with mobile-phase pH

Ionization efficiency is not flat across pH; it changes in response to mobile-phase pH and buffer chemistry. The UPLC-MS study reports that inducing complete deprotonation generates uniform carboxylate anions and synergistically enhances detection sensitivity [N5-R1]. The bile acid study likewise finds that ammonium levels and pH value affect negative electrospray ionization [N3-F2]. This means that ionization efficiency is a function of both pH and the mobile-phase environment, not just the analyte’s intrinsic pKa.

The evidence also implies that ionization efficiency can be optimized by choosing the right pH. If the analyte is protonated or deprotonated in a way that is unfavorable for ionization, detection response will be poor. If the analyte is in the optimal ionized form, detection sensitivity improves [N3-F2][N5-R1].

---

## 6) Detection response relates to ionization and mobile-phase chemistry

Detection response is tightly linked to ionization state and mobile-phase chemistry. The UPLC-MS study explains that its method uses a charge-state homogenization strategy guided by computational prediction of ionization behavior (pH/ionic forms) to optimize chromatographic and mass spectrometric conditions [N5-R1]. This indicates that detection response is not independent of pH; it depends on whether the analyte is in the correct ionized form and whether the mobile-phase chemistry supports efficient ionization.

The bile acid study also shows that ammonium levels and pH value affect negative electrospray ionization [N3-F2], reinforcing that detection response is not determined solely by the analyte’s intrinsic properties but also by the mobile-phase conditions used. This matters because bile acids are often analyzed by negative electrospray ionization (ESI), and their ionization efficiency can vary widely depending on pH and buffer chemistry [N3-F2].

---

## 7) Mobile-phase additives and buffers stabilize pH and ionization

Buffers are a key practical tool for controlling pH and stabilizing ionization. The branch report on mobile-phase additives and buffers states that buffers control pH to stabilize analyte ionization, improve peak shape, influence selectivity, ensure compatibility with detectors, and protect the stationary phase [N4-R3]. The same report notes that modifiers and pH interact with stationary-phase chemistry and that additive/buffer choice affects peak quality and selectivity [N4-F3].

This is especially relevant for bile acids because their ionization state is highly sensitive to buffer pH and ammonium level. The bile acid study reports that ammonium levels and pH value affect retention behaviors and ESI [N3-F2], and that volatile buffers with equivalent ammonium levels were used to demonstrate pH effects on retention [N3-F2]. This means that buffer selection should be guided by both separation and detection requirements.

---

## 8) Best practices: optimize pH for both separation and detection

The best practices branch report concludes that recommended buffer systems and pH ranges are chosen to balance separation, detection, and peak quality [N10]. The evidence supports a practical optimization strategy in which pH should be chosen to control retention and selectivity [N1-R1][N4-R3][N4-F3], while also stabilizing ionization and maximizing detection response [N6-R4][N5-R1][N3-F2].

The UPLC-MS study explicitly states that the method uses a charge-state homogenization strategy guided by pH/ionic-form prediction to optimize chromatographic and mass spectrometric conditions [N5-R1]. This is a strong example of how pH optimization is not just a retention problem; it is also a detection problem. The chromatography source cautions that mobile-phase pH can be a powerful tool to control retention and selectivity, but it can also get you in trouble if not controlled properly [N1-R1], which reinforces the need for careful method development.

---

## Conclusion

Overall, the evidence supports a unified conclusion: the mobile-phase pH influences chromatographic separation and ionization efficiency of bile acids in three main ways:

1. It changes the **ionization state** and **analyte charge**, which alters retention, selectivity, and detection response [N1-R1][N6-R4][N3-F2][N5-R1].
2. It affects the **interaction with the stationary phase** through changes in ionization state and buffer chemistry [N4-F3][N3-F2].
3. It improves **peak shape**, **resolution**, and **detection sensitivity** when chosen optimally [N1-R5][N4-R3][N5-R1].

For bile acid analysis, the best practice is therefore to use buffers to set pH and stabilize ionization, select organic modifiers that work well with the stationary phase and detection mode, and optimize pH jointly for both separation and detection [N4-R3][N3-F2][N4-F3][N5-R1].
